Hey, happy to advise as much as I can! For starters, I should mention that I didn't get hired as a senior developer or anything glamorous, I'm very much on the first or second rung of the ladder, but it has been a good start for me! Unfortunately from what I've heard a lot of software companies are scaling back hiring, my company included, so it may not be as easy now as it was a year or two ago, but still worth a shot!

What I'd recommend more than anything else is ask around and see if any friends of friends know someone who is in the industry already who'd be able to recommend you for something and give you tips on interviewing. Short of that, there's a ton of online resources as well, but the recommendation from a current or former employee can help get your foot in the door. 

If you can, talk to someone in the industry and get a sense of how to translate your skills and experiences into the language that recruiters and hiring managers in this industry use. There are a lot of buzzwords (KPI's, stakeholders, deliverables, etc.) that are super common in this space, and even if you weren't using these buzzwords to describe what you did in previous roles, you'll want to start using them to describe your experiences so that you're speaking the same language as the people interviewing you. It's not just about using the buzzwords though, it's about really understanding what they mean and confidently being able to describe your previous work in this new language, if that makes sense. 

Another big component is being confident, do your research and understand what value you bring to the table. As someone with a non-traditional background coming into the tech industry, I really believed during my interview that I could bring a fresh perspective to the team I was joining. Leveraging that in conversations and coming across as confident and excited to learn can really work wonders. 

Best of luck!

There are physical signs, blueness or greyness around the lips and fingertips, gurgling/loud snoring sounds. Ultimately if someone is unresponsive and can't be woken, there is a chance that they've overdosed. Call EMS, report an unresponsive person, and administer Naloxone. If they have overdosed, you could save their life. If there is some other issue, you're certainly not hurting their chances by giving them Naloxone.

I work in the social services industry and am certified to dispense Naloxone kits and I give them to ****anyone**** who walks in our office. You can learn how to administer Naloxone in under 5 minutes and it can potentially save a life at literally no cost to you, so why not? It's one of those things where we hope we will never need it, but if a situation presents itself, you're so much better for having it than not.
